en.heading: Moshe Rabbeinu begins explaining the Torah

paragraphs.text: The Rav opens with the beginning of Devarim, where Moshe Rabbeinu began to explain the Torah, which Rashi explains as making it understood in any language. This, he says, brought the Torah down to the understanding of Jews in whichever exile they find themselves. Each year on Rosh Chodesh Shevat a new flow of Torah comes down; it is Rosh Hashanah for the trees according to Beis Shammai, and the tree is the Eitz Chaim, the Torah.

Threads extend from Moshe Rabbeinu into every Jewish heart in every generation, the Rav explains. Every Jew who learns Torah is connected to him, even if the wire joining him to Moshe Rabbeinu's circuit is as thin as a thread.

en.heading: Many levels of souls, one source

paragraphs.text: The Rav turns to the Tanya's question: if the G-dly soul is truly a part of G-d above, and Hashem is one and indivisible, how can there be big souls and small souls? He answers that every soul is connected to the Ein Sof, the Infinite, but some merit direct contact while others are separated by levushim, garments. A high-voltage wire wrapped in enough insulation can be touched without feeling the current; so too everyone carries the current of the Ribono shel Olam.

The Tanya adds that there are levels within each person. The Rav lists five: nefesh at the bris or naming, ruach at bar mitzvah, neshamah at twenty for a married talmid chacham, though not all merit it, chayah in very special people, and yechidah, where all souls fuse into one, the level of Moshiach, of which David HaMelech speaks in Tehillim. So the question returns: if each is a part of G-d above, how can one be higher than another?

en.heading: Nails and hair: last to develop

paragraphs.text: To answer, the Rav describes how a child develops. The drop comes from the father's brain, and the brain forms first; then hands, feet, skin and sinews, and last of all the nails and hair. He brings the Gemara that a newborn is in doubt of viability for thirty days, but one born with nails and hair is known to be viable, since they need the full nine months.

Scientists, he notes, find the same chromosomes in the brain and in the nails and hair, yet the nails are removed from the source by nine months. In the same way, the Tanya's mashal teaches, souls come from the wisdom of the Ribono shel Olam: tzaddikim and talmidei chachamim are close like the eyes, others distant like the nails, through levushim upon levushim. And as excess nails are cut without the body feeling it, some parts of Klal Yisrael are cut off and do not feel it.

en.heading: No Jew is cut off; Erev Shabbos

paragraphs.text: The Rav reads the Tanya's line that even the low soul in the body of an am ha'aretz or a sinner is drawn from the heavenly mind, just as the toenails, the farthest part of the body, came from the same drop and stay bound to it. He brings the Gemara that Hashem gives the soul, the father the white parts such as bones, sinews and nails, and the mother the red parts; the nails come from the father, only they lingered longer.

He connects this to cutting hair and nails before Shabbos. The Mishnah in Sanhedrin lists those with no share in the World to Come, but the Gemara says every Jew has a share: theoretically one could be cut off, in fact never. The 36 sins carrying kareis are 36 threads binding a person to the Ribono shel Olam; each cuts one, the heavenly surgeon can reconnect it through teshuvah, and no Jew was ever liable on all 36.

So, the Rav says, Erev Shabbos the extra nails and hair, the goyishe part in oneself, are cut off, because every Shabbos is a new rise over the last. One regards oneself as a convert, cuts the nails and hair, and goes to the mikveh.

en.heading: A question, Achan, and Yisrael with Bereishis

paragraphs.text: A listener asks why there are halachos on handling cut nails. The Rav answers that the Mishnah speaks from what our minds grasp, but the Ribono shel Olam knows they remain connected; there is a point in every Jew that cannot be eradicated.

He then brings the Tzemach Tzedek on why the Gemara in Sanhedrin piles up Achan's sins: it expounds that though he sinned he is Yisrael, still connected. Yisrael, the last word of the Torah, is the lowest level, the nails and hair, and it is bound to Bereishis, the first word, the soul of Moshe Rabbeinu. Whatever is in the soul, he adds, is also in space and time, as Sefer Yetzirah says.

en.heading: Adar, the Megillah and the end of exile

paragraphs.text: In the calendar, Nisan corresponds to Moshe Rabbeinu, and the last month, Adar, to the generation before Moshiach: it has no open miracles. In the Megillah Hashem's name does not appear; 'the King' plainly means Achashverosh, just as in the newspapers one sees only the leaders, not the One pulling the strings. The only sign of fear of Heaven is Esther's call to fast.

The Megillah was written at the end of the Babylonian exile, when, as the Gemara in Megillah relates, even Daniel erred in counting the seventy years; that, the Rav says, is hester panim. When Moshiach comes everything will be understood. Now the heel of Moshiach is the nails and hair of the calendar, the end of the nine months, before the birth of Moshiach.

The Rav asks why the Tanya begins with 'madregos' and ends with the Aramaic 'dargin'. He brings the verse that Hashem cast a tardemah, a deep sleep, on Adam, and the Arizal's gematria that tardemah equals Targum. Man is human through his intellect and sinks lowest in sleep; the end of exile is such a sleep, far from the mind, at the heel.

Targum is the lowest level, so the Tanya can no longer say 'madregos' and switches to Targum; yet even these levels remain bound to the Ribono shel Olam. Yisrael holds lamed, the largest letter, and yud, the smallest, like the Megillah's 'from small to great'.
